p.title: Adaptive Submodularity: A New Approach to Active Learning and Stochastic Optimization

ext.title: Adaptive Submodularity: A New Approach to Active Learning and Stochastic Optimization
ext.venue: No venue printed in the text. Self-cited as Golovin & Krause (2010), CoRR abs/1003.3967 (arXiv preprint). Correction to the metadata hint: JAIR 42 (2011), 427-486 is a separate, longer article with the same arXiv ID (its text is at _text/6ba342dad525.txt per the manifest), not this 13-page text.
ext.document_type: Conference-style preprint (13 pages per manifest; theory paper, no experiments)
ext.coverage: Full text read in two chunks (lines 0-887, front matter through references; the file ends at the reference list). Every section was read: abstract, §1 intro, §2 setup, §3 adaptive submodularity (Defs 1-2, Prop 3), §4 greedy guarantee (Thm 4), §5 stochastic submodular maximization (Thm 5), §6 adaptive viral marketing (Thm 6), §7 active learning (Thm 7, Prop 8), §8 hardness (Thm 9), conclusions, references. No appendix or experiments section exists in this text. Proofs deferred to the extended version (Thm 7 proof, cost extensions) are not in the text and are reported as deferred. Paul's markup: checked. The manifest lists this PDF with n_annots = 0, and no JSON in _annots or annotations references ID 69ef3bf13239, so paul_markup is empty.
ext.research_question: When can a simple adaptive greedy policy be guaranteed near-optimal for stochastic optimization under partial observability, where feasible solutions are decision policies rather than sets? The paper defines adaptive submodularity as the policy-level analog of diminishing returns and asks which applications satisfy it (sensor placement with failures, adaptive viral marketing, pool-based active learning). It also asks how hard the general problem is without that property (§8).
ext.theory: Submodular set-function theory (Nemhauser, Wolsey & Fisher 1978) extended to policies. The key condition is that playing layer j of a policy tree earlier cannot decrease its marginal contribution (Def 2, Eq. 4). Equivalent form: for subrealizations Psi subset Psi', the expected marginal gain satisfies Delta_Psi'(e) <= Delta_Psi(e) (Prop 3, §3). Adaptive monotonicity is Def 1 (§3). Closure under nonnegative combinations and truncation is stated in §3.
ext.data: No dataset. Applications are analytic. (a) Sensor placement: finite location set E, sensor states O, independent failures P[Phi] = prod_e P[Phi(e)] (§5, p.6). (b) Adaptive viral marketing: directed graph G=(V,A) under the independent cascade model, with myopic or full-adoption feedback (§6, p.7). (c) Pool-based active learning: unlabeled pool X, finite hypothesis set H with prior p_H, binary or multi-class labels, no label noise (§7, p.8). No sample sizes, N, or period are reported.
ext.method: Analytic proofs only. Definitions of adaptive monotonicity and submodularity (Defs 1-2); derivative characterization (Prop 3, proof by constructing a path-shaped policy tree); greedy guarantee (Thm 4) via a telescoping argument adapted from Nemhauser et al. (1978) and Goundan & Schulz (2007); instantiations for three applications (Thm 5, Thm 6, Prop 8 / Thm 7); hardness via a reduction using a permanent-based puzzle and Feige & Lund (1997) (Thm 9).
ext.identification: Not applicable. There is no estimation or causal identification. The guarantees are worst-case bounds conditional on the prior P[Phi] and on the utility being adaptive submodular.
ext.scope: Population: none (no empirical units). Institution: none. Era: 2010 preprint. Domain: adaptive stochastic maximization and coverage, with examples in sensor placement, independent-cascade viral marketing (Kempe et al. 2003 model), and Bayesian pool-based active learning. Nothing in the text touches lobbying, elections, campaigns, legislators, persuasion or turnout, or text measurement. The only network-relevant content is §6 (influence spread on a directed graph with edge probabilities), which bears on seed allocation under a budget k.

key_findings.finding: Under adaptive monotonicity and adaptive submodularity, the alpha-approximate greedy policy achieves at least (1 - e^{-l/(alpha k)}) of the expected reward of the best policy with k items; with l = k and alpha = 1 this is the classic (1 - 1/e) guarantee.
If greedy can only be computed to additive error epsilon, the guarantee becomes (1 - e^{-l/k}) OPT - l*epsilon.

Sensor placement with multiple failure types (not only all-or-nothing failure) under independent failures is adaptive submodular, so the adaptive greedy policy achieves (1 - 1/e) of the best adaptive policy when the base objective f-hat is monotone submodular. This extends Asadpour et al. (2008).

Adaptive viral marketing under the independent cascade model is adaptive submodular for any nonnegative monotone submodular reward over influenced nodes, under both myopic and full-adoption feedback. The greedy seed policy therefore achieves (1 - 1/e) of the best policy. This generalizes Kempe et al. (2003) from a fixed seed set to adaptive seeding.

In the Bayesian pool-based active learning setting, generalized binary search (greedy version-space reduction) needs at most OPT * (ln(1/min_h p_H(h)) + 1) expected queries, improving the leading constant of the ln term to 1 relative to the prior analysis.
key_findings.location: Thm 7 (statement §7, p.8; proof deferred to extended version, lines 644-645)

key_findings.finding: A lower bound of (1/2 - epsilon) ln(1/min_h p_H(h)) holds for active learning under the complexity assumption NP not in DTIME(n^{O(log log n)}), so the constant in Thm 7 is close to tight.
key_findings.location: §7, p.8, lines 627-631 (reduction from Chakaravarthy et al. 2007 with Feige 1998)

key_findings.finding: Version-space reduction is adaptive monotone and adaptive submodular (Prop 8), which is the step that yields Thm 7.

Without adaptive submodularity the general Adaptive Stochastic Maximization problem is inapproximable: no polynomial-time algorithm with budget beta*k can approximate the reward of the optimal k-budget policy within O(|E|^{1 - epsilon/beta}), unless PH = Sigma2P. This holds even for pointwise linear objectives.
key_findings.numbers: approximation factor O(|E|^{1 - epsilon/beta}) for any epsilon > 0

key_findings.finding: With item costs, the greedy guarantee for active learning improves to ln(1/min p_H(h)) + 1 and removes the dependence on max/min cost ratios in the earlier bound of Guillory & Bilmes (O(log(|H| max c / min c))). The cost extension is stated but its proof is deferred to the extended version.
key_findings.numbers: ln(1/min p_H) + 1 vs earlier O(log(|H| max c / min c))

measures: marginal benefit Delta_Psi(e) = E[f(dom(Psi) union {e}, Phi) - f(dom(Psi), Phi) | Phi ~ Psi] (Eq. 5)
approximation ratio relative to the best policy with budget k (Thm 4, 5, 6)
expected number of queries relative to OPT (Thm 7)
stochastic dominance between random influenced-node sets S and S' (§6 proof)
limitations: Results are worst-case guarantees under a known Bayesian prior P[Phi]; no estimation from data or robustness to a misspecified prior is analyzed (§2, §5, §7).
Sensor placement guarantees (Thm 5) assume independent failures across locations, P[Phi] = prod_e P[Phi(e)] (§5, line 379).
Viral marketing (Thm 6) is analyzed under the independent cascade model only, with two feedback models (myopic and full-adoption) (§6, p.7).
Active learning (Thm 7) assumes no label noise and a finite hypothesis set H (§7, line 595).
Greedy may be computationally intractable in some applications; the guarantee then requires an alpha-approximate greedy rule with a loss factor alpha (§4, lines 256-259).
Proof of Thm 7 is deferred to the longer version, and the cost extensions and general adaptive stochastic coverage results are deferred to the extended version (lines 644-645, 625-626, 130-131).
Thm 9 is a worst-case hardness result under complexity-theoretic assumptions (PH != Sigma2P); it does not say how hard typical instances are.
No empirical evaluation or experiments are reported in this text.
Text does not mention lobbying, elections, legislators, persuasion/turnout, or text measurement, so its applicability to those domains is outside the paper.
references_of_note: Kempe, Kleinberg & Tardos (2003), Maximizing the spread of influence through a social network, KDD: the independent cascade model and monotone submodular spread (§1, §6). Most relevant to networks.
Nemhauser, Wolsey & Fisher (1978), analysis of approximations for maximizing submodular set functions I: greedy (1-1/e) guarantee the paper generalizes (§2).
Asadpour, Nazerzadeh & Saberi (2008), Stochastic submodular maximization, WINE: all-or-nothing sensor failure case, extended in Thm 5 (§5).
Krause & Guestrin (2007), Near-optimal observation selection using submodular functions, AAAI: submodular sensor-placement objectives (§1, §5).
Golovin & Krause (2010) extended version (CoRR abs/1003.3967): holds cost, general coverage, and deferred proofs (§7, §9).
Kosaraju, Przytycka & Borgstrom (1999), Dasgupta (2004), and Guillory & Bilmes (2009, 2010): greedy binary search / active learning bounds that Thm 7 improves (§7).
Feige (1998), threshold of ln n for set cover: 1-1/e is tight unless P = NP (§2, §7).
Goemans & Vondrak (2006), stochastic covering and adaptivity (§5). Minoux (1978): lazy evaluation of greedy marginal gains (§4).

short_quotes.quote: We prove that if a problem satisfies this property, a simple adaptive greedy algorithm is guaranteed to be competitive with the optimal policy.
Kempe et al. (2003) show that the set function which quantifies the expected number of nodes influenced is submodular.
Problems (1) is hard to approximate under reasonable complexity theoretic assumptions.

rel.summary_md:
Golovin and Krause extend the classic greedy guarantee for submodular sets (Nemhauser et al. 1978) to adaptive policies. In their setting you pick an item, observe its random outcome, and only then pick the next. Two properties are required. Adaptive monotonicity (Def 1) means an added item never lowers the expected reward. Adaptive submodularity (Prop 3) means an item's expected marginal gain only shrinks as more outcomes are observed. When both hold, the adaptive greedy policy achieves at least (1 - e^{-l/(alpha k)}) of the best k-item policy (Thm 4). With alpha = 1 and l = k this is 1 - 1/e, about 0.632. If marginals are estimated with additive error epsilon, the bound loses l*epsilon. The paper applies the result to three problems: sensors with independent failures (Thm 5), adaptive seeding under the independent cascade (Thm 6), and Bayesian active learning, where it gives an OPT*(ln(1/min p_H)+1) bound (Thm 7). Without adaptive submodularity, the general problem cannot be approximated within O(|E|^{1-epsilon/beta}) (Thm 9). This is a 13-page theory preprint with no data.

What it means for Paul's system: the CU budget optimizer and the frontier both run lazy greedy, but neither is adaptive in the paper's sense. Nothing is observed. Seed take-up is drawn inside Monte Carlo, and "conversions" are deterministic modeled transitions. The optimizer already scopes its claims correctly. In a fixed stance state it is exact (separable and concave), and once a conversion can happen it reports no guarantee, which Thm 9 supports. The sharpest finding is in the dashboard's budgetRecruit. It claims the full (1-1/e), but because it multiplies each candidate's gain by a target-proximity weight in [1,3], Thm 4 only supports about 0.28 when a target is set. The paper also defines the step the system has not built: seed one member, observe whether they took up the ask (SGATE), then re-plan.

bearings.paper_claim: Under adaptive monotonicity and adaptive submodularity, the alpha-approximate adaptive greedy gets >= (1 - e^{-l/(alpha k)}) of the best policy (1-1/e at alpha=1, l=k). Without adaptive submodularity, Adaptive Stochastic Maximization is inapproximable within O(|E|^{1-epsilon/beta}) unless PH = Sigma2P, even for pointwise-linear objectives.
bearings.system_side: The optimizer runs CELF lazy greedy in $500 steps. In a fixed stance state it certifies the exact grid optimum (separable, verified concave) and reports 1-1/e only as a 'worst_case_submodular_floor'. When a modeled money-triggered conversion is reachable, it rebuilds the queue, reports guarantee kind 'none', and explicitly refuses to call the run an observed adaptive policy. The G-K data-dependent bound is cited as 'JAIR'11 Lemma 5.3 / A.9'.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's adaptive guarantee needs a random state Phi that the policy observes, plus adaptive submodularity. The optimizer has no observation step: conversions are deterministic model thresholds. So Thm 4 does not apply to the replanning mode, and Thm 9's hardness explains why no guarantee should be claimed there. The code already does this. In fixed-state mode, separable concavity gives exactness, which is stronger than the paper's bound, so the paper adds nothing there. The cited Lemma 5.3/A.9 is not in this 13-page text. It belongs to the extended JAIR version (golovin-2011-adaptive-submodularity-theory).

bearings.paper_claim: An alpha-approximate greedy rule (each pick's marginal >= 1/alpha of the best marginal) only guarantees (1 - e^{-l/(alpha k)}) of optimal. The full (1-1/e) requires alpha = 1.
bearings.paper_location: Thm 4 and Def of alpha-approximate greedy, §4 p.5 (lines 256-259)
bearings.system_side: budgetRecruit maximizes a monotone submodular coverage sum_u [1 - prod(1-p)], and its comment claims 'the classic greedy keeps the (1-1/e)≈0.63 guarantee'. When a target is given, though, each candidate's true coverage marginal g is multiplied by (1 + 2*dT[c]). Here dT is max-product proximity in (0,1], so the multiplier lies in [1,3] and greedy picks argmax of weighted gain rather than of true marginal.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Pure math, so it carries over directly. With the target weighting, the chosen item's true marginal is >= 1/3 of the best, so alpha <= 3. Thm 4 then supports only about 1 - e^{-1/3} ≈ 0.28 of optimal coverage, not 0.63. With no target (dT null), the 1-1/e claim holds for this one-hop coverage objective. Note that the objective counts only one-hop coverage, not cascade spread. UNVERIFIED (agent analysis, single path, DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Greedy computed with additive marginal error epsilon guarantees (1 - e^{-l/k})·OPT - l·epsilon. Adaptive seeding is adaptive submodular (hence 1-1/e) for the single-colour independent cascade with any monotone submodular reward, under myopic or full-adoption feedback.
bearings.paper_location: §4 p.5 text after Thm 4 (lines 339-346); Thm 6, §6 p.7
bearings.system_side: The frontier runs lazy greedy up to 60 seeds on a Monte Carlo spread (MC=20, CRN). The spread comes from a two-colour competitive race with money-driven anti bystanders and seeds gated by contingent take-up. The marginal is max(0, sp - cur)*fac[c], with leverage and contest factors. Seeds are chosen before any take-up is observed, and the display curve is clamped because MC dips occur.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Thm 6 covers only single-colour IC. The frontier's competitive race with anti bystanders, plus the per-candidate fac weights, puts it outside that guarantee (see Bharathi/Borodin on competitive models). Even where submodularity held, the MC=20 noise in each marginal enters the bound as a -l*epsilon term over up to 60 seeds. The observed MC dips mean epsilon is not negligible. The knee should be read as a heuristic, not a certified diminishing-returns point.

bearings.paper_claim: When items fail independently (P[Phi] = prod_e P[Phi(e)]), and failure has multiple outcome types, the problem is adaptive submodular. Adaptive greedy, which places an item, observes its state, then continues, achieves (1-1/e) of the best ADAPTIVE policy (Thm 5). Adaptive seeding with feedback is likewise adaptive submodular (Thm 6).
bearings.system_side: gate(n) = max(0.15, seed_prob·SGATE[tier]) gives each lobbied seed a take-up probability. It is drawn independently per member on a dedicated CRN stream. The allocator never conditions later choices on whether earlier seeds actually took up the ask.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The gate already has the 'sensor with independent failure' structure that Thm 5 covers. An observe-then-replan policy (lobby, see whether the member moved, choose the next) would fall under the paper's guarantee, but only if take-up is independent across members and the reward stays adaptive submodular. In real Congresses, party whips and coalition timing correlate take-up, which violates the independence premise. SGATE values are themselves unestimated.

bearings.paper_claim: Kempe et al.'s expected-spread function is submodular, and the greedy guarantee applies to greedy SEQUENTIAL selection on true marginals (Thm 4 generalizes Nemhauser's greedy).
bearings.system_side: The coalition allocator computes SINGLETON marginals spread({n}) - base for the top-45, boosts them by (1+0.8 bpf), and water-fills dollars. It then honestly reports the joint spread against the naive-additive sum, because spread is submodular.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Reporting joint spread is correct and is consistent with submodularity. However, the allocation itself is not greedy on conditional marginals, so no (1-1/e) guarantee from this paper, or from Nemhauser, attaches to the per-topic seed sets. They are diagnostics, and the code already treats them as non-summable.

bearings.paper_claim: Once diminishing returns fail, no polynomial policy approximates the optimum within O(|E|^{1-epsilon/beta}) in the worst case (Thm 9). The positive results require adaptive submodularity.
bearings.system_side: Cheapest-tip LT priming sorts recruits greedily by $/influence-unit against tier thresholds theta. Threshold adoption is not submodular in general, and the code makes no approximation claim.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This is a worst-case statement only. It explains why no guarantee should be attached to LT priming or to any variant where pressure is non-diminishing. It says nothing about how typical instances on the cosponsor graph behave.

gaps_exposed: No observe-then-replan (adaptive) allocation. Seed take-up (SGATE) is only ever simulated inside Monte Carlo, never observed between choices, so the paper's adaptive guarantee, which compares against the best adaptive policy, is out of reach for every built allocator.
budgetRecruit's (1-1/e) comment ignores the alpha-approximation penalty from its (1+2*dT) target weighting. The supportable bound is about 0.28 when a target is set.
The Monte Carlo marginal error epsilon (MC=20, observed dips) is never bounded or propagated into the frontier's knee or guarantee language, even though Thm 4's corollary shows it costs l*epsilon.

No allocator tests whether its objective is adaptive submodular. The competitive two-colour race with anti bystanders falls outside Thm 6, and the system has no empirical check for diminishing returns on the spread objective; the optimizer checks concavity only for its own fixed-state separable objective.
The extended JAIR version (holding the data-dependent bound the code cites) is a separate document; the optimizer's citation 'JAIR'11 Lemma 5.3 / A.9' cannot be verified from this text.
flags: Citation scope: fec/engine/optimize.py:108 cites 'JAIR'11 Lemma 5.3 / A.9' for its data-dependent bound. That lemma is not in this 13-page CoRR preprint. Verify it against golovin-2011-adaptive-submodularity-theory before quoting the bound in any write-up.

Overclaim in the dashboard: make_dashboard_html_00.tpl:775-776 states the (1-1/e)≈0.63 guarantee for budgetRecruit. Under Thm 4 the target-weighted mode supports only about 1 - e^{-1/3} ≈ 0.28. UNVERIFIED (single agent path, DE-062) until reproduced.

Paul's Chen 2023 margin note says pressure from high-ranking members is 'not diminishing'. If that holds, adaptive submodularity fails and Thm 9's hardness applies, so any greedy (1-1/e) language on cascade-based allocators would be unsupported.
No conflict with the barred SNA proposals: the paper does not argue for dropping regular cosponsorship edges or for per-edge volume normalization, and it makes no LDA or reciprocity claims.
rel.paul_alignment: The evidence partly agrees with Paul, and his note is somewhat stale. He calls 'adaptive greedy plus CELF' the operational layer. The built optimizer uses CELF lazy greedy, but it is deliberately NOT adaptive. In a fixed stance state it is exact through separable concavity, which is stronger than Golovin-Krause, so the adaptive guarantee adds nothing there. In conversion mode it correctly claims no guarantee, which Thm 9 supports. The truly adaptive piece the paper describes would be lobbying, observing contingent take-up (the SGATE draw) and re-planning. That is not built, and the system's own docstring says so. Paul's expectation that GCOMB-style learned policies will replace greedy is outside this paper. His positions on per-topic-allocators and budget-frontier, which place them in a 'static and submodular tier', are partly right: the coalition allocator is not greedy on conditional marginals, and the frontier's competitive objective is not proven submodular.

related.why: This is the longer JAIR version with the same arXiv ID. It holds the proofs, cost extensions and the data-dependent bound (Lemma 5.3/A.9) that fec/engine/optimize.py cites.
Contingency-aware seeding, the basis of SGATE, is the adaptive-feedback setting that Golovin-Krause Thm 5/6 analyze, with independent take-up failures.
The competitive IC model behind the frontier's two-colour race falls outside the single-colour Thm 6 guarantee.
It shows that competitive threshold models can be non-submodular, which is where Thm 9's hardness, rather than Thm 4, applies (flip model, LT priming).
Complex contagion violates diminishing returns, so the adaptive-submodularity premise needed for greedy guarantees fails there.
The dashboard's closedCascadeRoute cites RELINK and correctly disclaims (1-1/e) for non-submodular IM-CSN, consistent with Thm 9.
Its empirical challenge to greedy in IM is a counterweight to the worst-case greedy guarantees here. The dashboard uses PageRank on that basis.
Greedy influence maximization under the independent cascade, the non-adaptive special case of Thm 6.
